triage.reason: Very common symptom-based diagnosis reachable by history and exam; good for teaching red flags and secondary causes.

age.peak: bimodal: young women in their 20s–30s and adults over 65

demographics: More common in women than men
Prevalence rises with age, especially after age 65
More common in people with lower income and lower fiber intake
Common in people who are bedbound or in long-term care

risk_factors.text: Ignoring the urge to have a bowel movement
Recent travel or change in routine

family_history: Family history of constipation or irritable bowel syndrome
exposures: Recent travel with change in diet or routine

chief_complaints.text: I haven't had a bowel movement in days
My poop is hard and dry
I have to strain to go

hpi.onset: Gradual over days to weeks; often chronic and intermittent over months
hpi.duration: Usually days to weeks for acute episodes; chronic if present for more than 3 months
hpi.progression: Slowly worsens as stool becomes harder and more difficult to pass; may improve with diet changes or laxatives
hpi.location: Lower abdomen, often left lower quadrant

associated_symptoms.text: Rectal bleeding from hemorrhoids or fissure

pertinent_negatives: Blood in stool (other than streaks from hemorrhoids)
Recent travel to areas with poor sanitation

argues_against: Neurologic deficits suggesting spinal cord lesion

atypical.how_it_differs: Present with crying during bowel movements, hard stools, or infrequent stools; may have anal fissure. Often related to diet transitions or formula.
Often present with withholding behavior, soiling, abdominal pain, or urinary symptoms; may have a history of painful bowel movements leading to fear of going.
More likely to have multiple contributing factors including medications, immobility, and comorbid conditions; may present with overflow incontinence or fecal impaction.
Very common due to hormonal changes and pressure from the uterus; may present with hemorrhoids and rectal bleeding.
May have more severe or atypical infections causing constipation, such as Clostridioides difficile or other pathogens; consider infectious causes.
May be due to autonomic neuropathy; often chronic and resistant to usual treatments.
Often associated with low fiber intake and sedentary lifestyle; may be part of metabolic syndrome.

general.severe: Ill-appearing, diaphoretic, lying still due to pain

findings.finding: Mild, diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound
Palpable stool in the descending or sigmoid colon
Hard stool in the rectal vault

labs.caveat: Hypothyroidism is a treatable cause of chronic constipation; a normal TSH makes it unlikely.
Hypercalcemia causes constipation and can be from malignancy or hyperparathyroidism.
Hypokalemia slows bowel motility; often from diuretics or vomiting.
Dehydration or renal impairment can contribute; guides safe laxative use.
Elevated from dehydration or poor intake.
Anemia raises concern for colorectal cancer or other chronic disease, especially in older adults.
Microcytosis suggests iron deficiency, which may accompany occult gastrointestinal blood loss.
Low ferritin supports iron deficiency and warrants evaluation for gastrointestinal blood loss.
Leukocytosis is uncommon in simple constipation and suggests an alternative diagnosis such as infection or ischemia.
Diabetes can cause autonomic neuropathy and chronic constipation.
Order in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or laxatives; pregnancy itself causes constipation and changes management.
Elevation is not expected in simple constipation and should prompt evaluation for inflammation or infection.

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected fecal impaction or bowel obstruction when the diagnosis is unclear

findings.text: Large amount of stool throughout the colon, especially the rectum and sigmoid
Dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels suggesting obstruction

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Red flags such as weight loss, severe pain, or suspected obstruction or malignancy

findings.text: Colonic stool burden with a dilated colon
Colonic mass or stricture causing obstruction
Proximal colonic dilation with a transition point (obstruction)

imaging.preferred_when: Adults with alarm features or age-appropriate colorectal cancer screening
Chronic constipation not responding to treatment, to assess pelvic floor function

findings.text: Impaired relaxation of the anal sphincter or absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex (dyssynergic defecation)

initial.why: Looks for anemia or leukocytosis suggesting bleeding, infection, or malignancy
Checks potassium, calcium, and kidney function as reversible contributors
Hypothyroidism is a common treatable cause of chronic constipation
Pregnancy causes constipation and changes safe treatment choices

confirmatory.why: Confirms a large stool burden or suggests obstruction when the diagnosis is uncertain

supporting.why: Identifies diabetes as a cause of autonomic neuropathy
supporting.only_if: chronic constipation or risk factors for diabetes

supporting.why: Evaluates for iron deficiency from occult gastrointestinal blood loss
Screens for inflammation when infection or ischemia is a concern
supporting.only_if: fever, severe pain, or systemic symptoms

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.why: Evaluates for obstruction, mass, or other structural cause
supporting.only_if: alarm features such as weight loss, severe pain, or suspected obstruction

supporting.why: Evaluates for colorectal cancer, stricture, or other mucosal disease
supporting.only_if: alarm features or age-appropriate colorectal cancer screening

not_indicated.why: Not needed for typical constipation without concern for impaction or obstruction

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

not_indicated.why: Not routine without alarm features or screening indication
Reserved for chronic constipation that does not respond to treatment
No role unless pancreatitis is suspected
Not needed unless urinary symptoms suggest another cause

decision_points: Check for alarm features (rectal bleeding, weight loss, anemia, new onset after age 50) before treating as simple constipation
Pregnancy test before imaging or laxatives in anyone who could be pregnant
Digital rectal exam is essential to detect impaction, mass, or fissure
Consider medication review for opioids, iron, anticholinergics, and calcium channel blockers

criteria.name: Rome IV criteria for functional constipation (paraphrased)
criteria.summary: Two or more of: straining, hard stools, incomplete evacuation, sensation of blockage, manual maneuvers to pass stool, or fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements per week, present for at least three months with symptom onset at least six months earlier, and not explained by another condition.
items: Straining with more than a quarter of bowel movements
Hard or lumpy stools in more than a quarter of bowel movements
Sensation of incomplete evacuation in more than a quarter of bowel movements
Sensation of anorectal blockage in more than a quarter of bowel movements
Manual maneuvers to help pass stool in more than a quarter of bowel movements
Fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements per week

differential.name: Colorectal cancer
differential.why_considered: A colonic mass can narrow the lumen and cause progressively worsening constipation, especially in older adults.
differential.trigger: New constipation after age 50, rectal bleeding, unintentional weight loss, or iron deficiency anemia

history: Rectal bleeding or blood mixed with stool
exam: Rectal mass on digital rectal exam
labs: Iron deficiency anemia with low ferritin and low MCV
imaging: Colonic mass or stricture on CT or colonoscopy

differential.name: Bowel obstruction
differential.why_considered: Constipation with abdominal pain and distension can be the presenting picture of a mechanical obstruction.
differential.trigger: Inability to pass gas, vomiting, severe distension, or prior abdominal surgery

history: Inability to pass gas or stool
imaging: Dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels on x-ray

differential.name: Irritable bowel syndrome with constipation
differential.why_considered: Chronic constipation with abdominal pain and bloating is common in IBS-C and overlaps with functional constipation.

history: Recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation
Alternating constipation and diarrhea over time
Symptoms for years with no alarm features

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Slowed metabolism and gut motility from hypothyroidism can cause chronic constipation.

exam: Delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4

differential.name: Hypercalcemia
differential.why_considered: Elevated calcium slows bowel motility and can present with constipation, especially in malignancy or hyperparathyroidism.

history: History of cancer or kidney stones

differential.name: Fecal impaction
differential.why_considered: A hard stool mass in the rectum can cause obstruction-like symptoms and overflow incontinence, especially in older or immobile patients.

history: No bowel movement for many days
exam: Hard stool palpable in the rectal vault on digital rectal exam
Palpable stool in the left lower quadrant
imaging: Large stool burden in the rectum and sigmoid on abdominal x-ray

differential.name: Medication-induced constipation
differential.why_considered: Many common medications slow gut motility and are a frequent reversible cause of constipation.

history: Recent start or dose increase of opioids, iron, calcium channel blockers, anticholinergics, or diuretics
Temporal relationship between medication change and symptom onset

severity.mild: Infrequent hard stools with mild straining and bloating; patient is comfortable, no distension, normal vitals, and symptoms respond to diet and lifestyle changes.
severity.moderate: Persistent constipation with abdominal discomfort, bloating, and distension; may have palpable stool or mild tenderness; no systemic symptoms or alarm features.
severity.severe: Marked distension and pain with inability to pass stool despite laxatives; may have vomiting or signs of impaction; requires urgent evaluation for obstruction.
severity.critical: Constipation complicated by bowel obstruction, perforation, or sepsis with hemodynamic instability; life-threatening and requires emergency intervention.

red_flags.finding: Rectal bleeding or blood mixed with stool
red_flags.meaning: Suggests colorectal cancer, ischemia, or other serious mucosal disease; needs evaluation
Raises concern for malignancy or chronic disease

red_flags.finding: Inability to pass gas or stool with vomiting
red_flags.meaning: Suggests bowel obstruction; urgent imaging and surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Severe constant abdominal pain or peritoneal signs
red_flags.meaning: Suggests perforation, ischemia, or peritonitis; emergency
Suggests occult gastrointestinal blood loss, possibly from colorectal cancer
Suggests infection, ischemia, or perforation rather than simple constipation

complications.name: Fecal impaction
clues: No bowel movement for many days
Hard stool on digital rectal exam

complications.name: Hemorrhoids and anal fissure
clues: Bright red blood on toilet paper

special_populations.differences: Often present with withholding behavior, soiling, abdominal pain, or urinary symptoms; may have a history of painful bowel movements leading to fear of going. Treatment focuses on education, toilet training, and disimpaction.

Present with crying during bowel movements, hard stools, or infrequent stools; may have anal fissure. Often related to diet transitions or formula. Breastfed infants may normally have infrequent stools.

More likely to have multiple contributing factors including medications, immobility, and comorbid conditions; may present with overflow incontinence or fecal impaction. Higher risk of colorectal cancer and obstruction.

Very common due to hormonal changes and pressure from the uterus; may present with hemorrhoids and rectal bleeding. Treatment focuses on fiber, fluids, and safe laxatives; avoid stimulant laxatives unless advised.
May be due to autonomic neuropathy; often chronic and resistant to usual treatments. Evaluate for other causes and optimize glycemic control.
Often associated with low fiber intake and sedentary lifestyle; may be part of metabolic syndrome. Weight loss and increased activity can help.

key_questions.question: How many bowel movements have you had in the past week?
key_questions.looking_for: Fewer than three per week suggests constipation; a normal frequency argues against it

key_questions.question: When did this start, and has it been getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over days to weeks; new or progressive change in a person over 50 raises concern for a structural cause

key_questions.question: What do your stools look like — hard, lumpy, or dry?
key_questions.looking_for: Hard or lumpy stools support the diagnosis

key_questions.question: Do you have to strain, or feel like you cannot completely empty?
key_questions.looking_for: Straining and incomplete evacuation are core features

key_questions.question: Does it hurt to pass stool, or have you seen blood on the toilet paper?
key_questions.looking_for: Painful passage or bright red streaks suggest hemorrhoids or an anal fissure; blood mixed with stool is a red flag

key_questions.question: Have you been unable to pass gas, or had vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Inability to pass gas or stool with vomiting suggests bowel obstruction and needs urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss raises concern for malignancy or chronic disease

key_questions.question: Any fever, severe constant pain, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests infection, ischemia, or another serious cause rather than simple constipation

key_questions.question: What do you usually eat and drink in a day?
key_questions.looking_for: Low fiber and low fluid intake are common reversible contributors

key_questions.question: How much do you move around during the day?
key_questions.looking_for: Sedentary lifestyle or immobility slows bowel motility

key_questions.question: Do you ever hold it in or ignore the urge to go?
key_questions.looking_for: Ignoring the urge is a common behavioral contributor, especially in children and busy adults

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including anything for pain, iron, or allergies?
key_questions.looking_for: Opioids, iron, calcium carbonate, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers, and diuretics are common causes

key_questions.question: Have you had abdominal or pelvic surgery before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior surgery raises concern for adhesions or obstruction

key_questions.question: Do you have thyroid problems, diabetes, or Parkinson disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypothyroidism, diabetes with autonomic neuropathy, and Parkinson disease cause chronic constipation

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have constipation, IBS, or colon cancer?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of constipation or IBS; colon cancer raises concern for a structural cause

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy causes constipation and changes safe treatment choices

key_questions.question: Any burning with urination, blood in the urine, or trouble urinating?
key_questions.looking_for: Urinary symptoms may point to another cause or to pelvic floor dysfunction

key_questions.question: Any weakness, numbness, or trouble walking?
key_questions.looking_for: Neurologic deficits suggest a spinal cord lesion rather than simple constipation

reasoning_points: Fewer than three bowel movements per week with hard stools, straining, or incomplete evacuation
Symptoms are chronic or recurrent rather than a single episode
No alarm features: no rectal bleeding, weight loss, fever, vomiting, or inability to pass gas
Medication review identifies or excludes opioids, iron, anticholinergics, and calcium channel blockers
Reversible causes considered and checked: hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, dehydration, pregnancy
Digital rectal exam performed to look for impaction, mass, or fissure
Red flags prompt evaluation for obstruction or colorectal cancer rather than routine treatment

easy: Young adult with low fiber and fluid intake
Fewer than three bowel movements a week with hard stools
No alarm features and normal vitals
medium: Older adult on multiple medications including an opioid or calcium channel blocker
Chronic constipation with intermittent abdominal pain and bloating suggesting IBS-C
Pregnancy with hemorrhoids and rectal bleeding
Hypothyroidism or hypercalcemia found on labs
hard: Older adult with new constipation, weight loss, and iron deficiency anemia suggesting colorectal cancer
Patient with vomiting and inability to pass gas suggesting bowel obstruction
Older or immobile patient with overflow incontinence from fecal impaction
Child with withholding behavior and soiling rather than a clear complaint of constipation
